prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: a severe immunocompromised state (asplenia and untreated hypogammaglobulinemia) is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).
Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of the immunocompromised state (asplenia and hypogammaglobulinemia) (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a severe immunocompromised state (asplenia and untreated hypogammaglobulinemia) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: stop ampicillin and continue ceftriaxone (or benzylpenicillin; penicillin MIC 0.06 ug/mL, susceptible) for 14 days for Streptococcus pneumoniae (NICE NG240).
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.

Recognise asplenia with hypogammaglobulinemia: after recovery give pneumococcal, meningococcal (ACWY and B) and Hib vaccination, and refer to clinical immunology to assess immunoglobulin replacement after a second invasive pneumococcal infection.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
Echocardiography is not part of the meningitis work-up; nothing in the case suggests endocarditis.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, partially treated, in an asplenic patient

differential.key_features: Excluded: neutrophilic CSF (392 cells/uL, 72% neutrophils) with a glucose ratio of 0.22 and lactate 6.8 mmol/L; Streptococcus pneumoniae on CSF PCR and in blood cultures; viral panel targets not detected.
No seizures or focal deficit; HSV-1 and HSV-2 not detected on CSF PCR; neutrophilic CSF with a bacterial isolate.

differential.diagnosis: Sinusitis with parameningeal spread (subdural empyema or brain abscess)
differential.key_features: Maxillary sinus mucosal thickening on CT may be the source, but CT shows no extra-axial collection or parenchymal lesion; MRI only if he fails to improve.
Subacute onset, lymphocytic CSF and basal enhancement; here a 24-hour course with neutrophilic CSF and a pyogenic isolate.
Headache built up over hours with fever and meningism rather than a thunderclap onset; no hemorrhage on CT; CSF RBC 2 cells/uL; the faint yellow tinge accompanies a CSF protein of 153 mg/dL.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a severe immunocompromised state (asplenia and untreated hypogammaglobulinemia) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

Asplenia (anatomic or functional) dramatically increases risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); these patients require lifelong vaccination and a low threshold for empiric antibiotics.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior antibiotics reduce Gram-stain sensitivity and can sterilise the CSF; with neutrophilic pleocytosis, a low CSF:blood glucose ratio, raised CSF lactate and a positive pneumococcal PCR, the diagnosis remains bacterial meningitis.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative CSF Gram stain in a patient with prior oral antibiotic exposure
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest viral or aseptic meningitis and lower the threshold for withholding empiric antibiotics.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatremia is a common complication of bacterial meningitis itself (SIADH or cerebral salt wasting); assess volume status and correct it cautiously while the infection is treated. It does not point away from meningitis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect workup toward primary endocrine or volume-status causes of hyponatremia.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Parameningeal sinus disease can be a SOURCE of pneumococcal meningitis, not an alternative diagnosis; the CSF profile remains the deciding evidence.
red_herrings.data_point: Incidental bilateral maxillary sinus mucosal thickening on CT
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest uncomplicated sinusitis as the source of headache and fever, deferring meningitis evaluation.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: a severe immunocompromised state (asplenia and untreated hypogammaglobulinemia). NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (immunodeficiency); its 1.4.7 trigger of a progressive and sustained fall in level of consciousness is also met. Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

clinical_pearls: Asplenic patients should receive empiric coverage for encapsulated organisms whenever meningitis is suspected, with a very low threshold for LP and empiric antibiotics
A negative Gram stain in the context of prior antibiotic therapy does not rule out bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR retains sensitivity
The CSF-to-blood glucose ratio is more diagnostically useful than the absolute CSF glucose level; a ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low
Dexamethasone reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis from approximately 34% to 14% when given before or with the first dose of antibiotics (de Gans, NEJM 2002)

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Gerald Hamill is a 55-year-old right-handed man with a history of post-traumatic splenectomy, hypogammaglobulinemia, and hypertension who presents to the emergency department brought by his wife after progressive confusion and worsening headache over the past 24 hours. His wife reports that he developed a sore throat and mild cough approximately four days ago and was seen by his primary care physician two days prior to presentation, at which time he was diagnosed with a presumed upper respiratory tract infection and started on oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily. He initially seemed to improve slightly, but yesterday morning he began complaining of a severe, rapidly worsening diffuse headache. He took acetaminophen with minimal relief. By yesterday evening, his wife noticed he was becoming increasingly drowsy and was not making sense in conversation, intermittently confusing the names of their grandchildren and asking repetitive questions. She checked his temperature overnight and recorded 38.9 degrees Celsius at approximately 02:00 this morning. He developed rigors and was shaking in bed. She also noted that he seemed to be wincing when she turned on the bedroom light, pulling the blankets over his head. By this morning, he was difficult to fully rouse and she became alarmed and called emergency services. On arrival, paramedics found him lethargic with a GCS of 12. In the emergency department, he intermittently opens his eyes to voice and can state his name but is confused about his location and the date. He complains of severe neck pain and photophobia when asked. He denies any recent travel, sick contacts beyond his initial URI symptoms, or trauma. His wife confirms he has not received pneumococcal or meningococcal vaccinations despite his asplenic status, something their primary care physician had discussed but they had not yet followed up on. She also recalls his previous episode of pneumococcal pneumonia three years ago that required hospitalization.

neurological_exam.additional: Marked nuchal rigidity present. Kernig sign is positive bilaterally — patient grimaces and resists knee extension when hip is flexed to 90 degrees. Brudzinski sign is equivocal — subtle hip flexion noted with passive neck flexion. No petechiae or purpura on skin examination. No lymphadenopathy.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, sluggishly reactive. Visual fields unable to be reliably tested due to decreased level of consciousness. No obvious gaze deviation. Mild bilateral facial grimace to painful stimulation, symmetric. Gag reflex intact. No obvious facial asymmetry. Fundoscopic exam limited by patient cooperation; no gross papilledema appreciated but exam is suboptimal.
neurological_exam.gait: Not assessed — patient is too somnolent to stand.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Level of consciousness has fallen progressively over about 24 hours: alert at baseline, drowsy and confused by yesterday evening, difficult to rouse this morning, GCS 12 on arrival. Drowsy but arousable to voice. Oriented to person but uncertain about place and date. He does not follow one-step commands; he localizes to supraorbital pressure. Speech is slow and dysarthric but language content is appropriate when he responds. Unable to perform serial sevens or spell words backward due to inattention and somnolence. GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5).
neurological_exam.motor: Moves all four extremities spontaneously but less than expected. Withdraws symmetrically to noxious stimulation in all extremities. No focal motor deficit identified. No pronator drift assessable due to inattention. Tone mildly increased diffusely.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are equivocal bilaterally — neither clearly upgoing nor downgoing.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws to pain symmetrically in all extremities. Light touch examination unreliable due to altered mental status.
